newsitem.title: UK: NatWest Eurobonds seen unscathed after bank review.
newsitem.headline: NatWest Eurobonds seen unscathed after bank review.

text.p: NatWest Market's small but apparently profitable Eurobonds division should be little affected by the British bank's eagerly awaited strategic review, bankers said.
"For a very long time NatWest has concentrated on the long end of sterling, securitisation and sterling floaters," a banker familiar with its operations said.
"Their strategy on that side is already made for them. Unless they decide to pull out of those markets, which is very unlikely, I don't see there will be much of a change."

Latest data from Capital DATA Bondware showed NatWest Markets, the investment banking arm of Britain's National Westminster Bank, ranked 36th in a table of all Eurobond underwriters for the first six months of 1997, down from 24th place in the whole of 1996.
In the first half of this year, NatWest underwrote some $2.8 billion of international bond issues. All, apart from $230 million worth in dollars, was denominated in sterling.
Officials at NatWest, expected to unveil a new investment banking strategy in the coming weeks, have repeatedly denied speculation that the bank has plans to slim down its Eurobond operations.
"Historically we have not been a big factor outside sterling," a NatWest Markets spokeswoman said. "We have not pulled out of anything."
During 1996, NatWest Markets underwrote $5.0 billion equivalent in sterling, $2.8 billion in dollars, $156 million in pesetas and $80 million in Australian dollars.

Its league table standing in 1996 was boosted by a $5.0 billion securitisation underwritten by NatWest Markets. The highly innovative deal turned high-quality, low-margin corporate syndicated loans into securities, and freed around 200 million stg of capital for NatWest.

Industry analysts said because NatWest's Eurobond activities have been concentrated on a small number of sectors, they had also been profitable. Other banks which try to break into new sectors often subsidise deals to make inroads into the highly competitive market.

"NatWest's concentration has allowed them to be relatively profitable on the new issues side," the banker said. "They do trade fixed-rate dollars, and this book might be closed down in the review. They might lose some of their government bond sales people (in the review)."
Bankers said NatWest also traded Australian dollar Eurobonds.

NatWest has already said that profits will not be more than 770 million stg in the first half because of the underperformance of NatWest Markets, which has revealed a 77 million stg net loss on interest rate options.

Analysts will be looking for a clear strategic statement from NatWest chief executive Derek Wanless, who has temporarily taken command at NatWest Markets after its head Martin Owen resigned over the options losses.
In an effort to expand into the U.S. bond market, NatWest bought Greenwich Capital. "The idea behind the Greenwich team coming in was to gradually build a business," the NatWest official said.

"We are building a good franchise in the U.S. market, in high-yield and securitisation. When we acquired Greenwich it was to help us develop our presence in the U.S. and to use as a platform to build the business. And that is still the aim," she said.
